IT is impossible for anyone to guess at the future of the Highlands, or even to judge what will happen within the next few years, but most of those who have ties with Scotland, whether ties of birth or upbringing, or love of a region vested with the glamour of association with great historical movements of the past, must entertain ideals and expectations with the hope that they may one day become reality. The economic history of the Highlands is fairly broad in outline.

location_standardised: Switzerland
brief_context: Mentioned as an example of a country with a strong tourist industry.
brief_extract: There are, of course, other disappearing industries, such as the old handicraft industries associated with woollen textiles, hand-weaving, wood and leather working, but against all this must be set the active assets of the Highlands, chief of which is the tourist industry. Switzerland almost lives by its tourist industry, and this industry in the Highlands could be greatly increased. Already it is developing rapidly, and its limits cannot at present be foreseen.

location_standardised: Norway
brief_context: Mentioned as an example of successful afforestation and forest industries.
brief_extract: Again, there are the forests, which, though many were planted originally by the deer-stalking fraternity in their own interests and with a complete disregard of revenue-earning possibilities, could be converted into marketable timber if some development plan in connection with afforestation were to be formed by the Forestry Commissioners. Norway and Sweden show how afforestation and the attendance on existing forests is not only an industry in itself, but the basis of other industries. It is something to which agricultural landowners are able to turn during the season when farming makes least claim on them.

location_standardised: Simplon Tunnel, Valais, Switzerland

brief_extract:

time carried on from twenty-two points.

location_standardised: Loch Treig, Highland, Scotland, United Kingdom
brief_context: Source for water tunnel and raising of water level.
brief_extract:
This amazing
engineering feat necessitated the removal of one and a
half million tons of rock. The purpose of the tunnel is
to carry the waters of Loch Treig—which enter it at a
depth of one hundred feet below the surface—and
numerous side streams to a point where it emerges on
the mountain side above Fort William. From this point
two welded steel pipes, five feet nine inches in diameter,
run steeply down to the power station below with its
108,000 kilowatt capacity.

It is a
universally active force which depends for its wealth-
earning power on the speed with which it is universally
applied. One can see now the ancient land of Badenoch,
the home of the earliest Scottish clan, traversed by the
towers and poles carrying this new force, and if to that
force is added determination to bring back the old
agricultural economy and to strengthen it by everything
modern science can contribute, then one may in the pro-
cess of years see an even more rapid process of revival. Every intelligent person must agree that the only

authority, with full executive powers and representing
public opinion.

location_standardised: Italian Alps, Italy
brief_context: Reference for attractive building design in the Highlands.
brief_extract:
Under such an authority, determined to
work for the public good, the deserted landscapes of the
Highlands would become associated with intensive agri-
cultural development, aided by a far-seeing policy of
afforestation. There would be new communities, with
well-designed houses, centres for the marketing of agri-
cultural products and for the local industries dependent
on agriculture; there would be new tourist centres com-
posed of buildings as attractive and as well-designed as
those in the Swiss, Austrian or Italian Alps; efficient
road and railway communications, and new seaside
resorts, more peaceful and more beautiful than the
English South Coast towns, because they would be linked
up with the glens and the valleys; the widespread use
of water power would foster new industries; the produce
of the fishing villages would be efficiently marketed by
a central organisation; game and fishing preserves and
the deer forests would be utilised for the benefit of the
tourist industry; there would be new schools, new tech-
nical and agricultural colleges; communications between
the islands and the mainland would be improved. If
these improvements were intelligently and courageously
planned and carried through, the Highlands could be-
come economically sound and prosperous and, moreover,
one of the greatest playgrounds in Europe.

article_title: AN HISTORICAL LINK Between the Rayon Industry and the Electric Lighting Industry
brief_extract: For those who care to trace inventions to their source and study the working of an inventor's mind, the story is an interesting one. In December, 1878, the members of the Newcastle Chemical Society were shown a new form of electric lamp, quite different from the arc lamp which at that date was the only known means of lighting by electricity. This lamp was the invention of my father, Joseph Wilson Swan, whose inventions in the photographic field, notably the carbon process, bromide printing paper and a rapid dry plate, had already distinguished him as an inventor of uncommon versatility.

location_standardised: South Kensington, London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location where a replica of Swan's lamp is displayed.
article_title: AN HISTORICAL LINK Between the Rayon Industry and the Electric Lighting Industry
brief_extract: This lamp was the invention of my father, Joseph Wilson Swan, whose inventions in the photographic field, notably the carbon process, bromide printing paper and a rapid dry plate, had already distinguished him as an inventor of uncommon versatility. The lamp (a replica of which may be seen in the South Kensington Science Museum) was a cigar-shaped glass container with platinum terminals at each end supporting a very thin carbon rod. The air had been exhausted as completely as possible so as to produce the best vacuum obtainable in those days.

location_standardised: Denver, Colorado, United States
brief_context: City at the foot of the Rocky Mountains.
brief_extract:
We found the bus ride from Chicago westwards, three days over wheat-bearing plains, which were suffering from drought, oppressively hot. When we reached Denver, over 5,000 feet above sea level, at the foot of the Rocky Mountains, we were amused to find it advertised as "the mile-high city, air-conditioned by Nature."
We spent some days at Colorado Springs, a few miles from Denver, a charming small town where it was pleasant to walk on the mountains, to see pretty water-falls and to take a motor trip to the summit of Pike's Peak, a mountain over fourteen thousand feet high, with lovely views over the Rocky Mountain Range. Then we went through New Mexico, past flat-topped hills and dry-looking plains to Santa Fé, a Spanish capital before the time of the Pilgrim Fathers.

DEMONSTRATION HOUSE, BIRMINGHAM
The Birmingham Corporation Electricity Department, with the collaboration of the Birmingham Branch, equipped an electrical demonstration house at Warren Farm Road, on the Kingstanding Estate, which proved a great success; over 6,000 people visited the house dur- ing the month of exhibition, and many enquiries were received. article_title: The Coronation of Their Majesties King George VI and Queen Elizabeth
brief_extract:
1937

THE Coronation of Their Majesties King George VI and Queen Elizabeth next month in Westminster Abbey signals with traditional ceremony the beginning of a new reign, and with the many thousand visitors present from the Dominions and Colonies, it will be a more essentially " Empire " Coronation than any that have gone before. A quick comparison with last Coronation year shows amazing differences in the amenities of life then and now.

location_standardised: New South Wales, Australia

article_title: The Coronation of Their Majesties King George VI and Queen Elizabeth
brief_extract: In this magazine we have tried to indicate the varied and inestimable services electricity is rendering to the Empire economically, socially, and, through broadcasting, news films and quick transport, as the means to an ever closer sympathy between people separated by much of the earth's surface. The Electrical Association for Women cannot yet boast an Empire-wide organisation, but there are many overseas members, and an active sister Association is established in New South Wales. There is undoubtedly a universal and growing interest in the advantages offered by science to housecraft, and in this we are given a lead by H.M.

location_standardised: Wembley, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Site of the 1925 International Conference of Women.
article_title: The Coronation of Their Majesties King George VI and Queen Elizabeth
brief_extract:
Both she and His Majesty have always given and no doubt will continue to give encouragement to all forms of progress that may be of public service. At Wembley in 1925, when the Women's Engineering Society, parent of the E.A.W., organised the first International Conference of Women in Science, Industry and Commerce, the Duchess of York, now our Queen, presided at the Conference and gave her recognition to " the ever increasing scope of women's work."

The British Empire is fortunate in having at its head a King and Queen who have so closely at heart their people's good. May the reign of Their Majesties George VI and Elizabeth be a long, happy, peaceful and prosperous one.

article_title: A NEW AID FOR THE FARMER: A Description of some of the Uses of Electricity in Agriculture
brief_extract:
E. ROWLAND, A.M.I.E.E

A Description of some of the Uses
of Electricity in Agriculture

WITH the expansion of electricity supply in rural
areas, its use on farms has increased greatly
in recent years throughout the Empire, and
whereas only a short time ago electrical apparatus on
farms was a rarity, to-day it is by no means unusual,
and, in fact, in many parts it is almost commonplace. It is impossible to review the Empire in detail in the
space available, particularly as conditions vary widely
in different parts of the world.

location_standardised: New Zealand
brief_context: Example of electricity generated from water power for agriculture.
article_title: A NEW AID FOR THE FARMER: A Description of some of the Uses of Electricity in Agriculture
brief_extract:
It is impossible to review the Empire in detail in the
space available, particularly as conditions vary widely
in different parts of the world. As an example of the
part electricity is playing in various countries, mention
might be made of New Zealand, where electricity gener-
ated from water power is used extensively for agricul-
tural purposes. There are no less than 20,000 milking
machines in use in New Zealand, where the dairy indus-
try depends largely on them.

location_standardised: United Kingdom
brief_context: Refers to electrical development conditions within the United Kingdom.
article_title: A NEW AID FOR THE FARMER: A Description of some of the Uses of Electricity in Agriculture
brief_extract:
A great proportion of
these machines is driven electrically, and in conjunction
with them electricity is used for heating water for
washing up, and to generate steam for sterilising utensils. Below, reference is made to conditions at home, and,
although development varies in other parts of the
Empire, some of the subjects referred to are applic-
able to other countries. LIGHTING
As in other spheres, the use of electricity which
makes the first appeal is for lighting, and when
it is remembered that the only alternative forms of
lighting in farm buildings are hurricane lamps or candles,
and in the farmhouse candles or oil lamps, it will be
appreciated what a tremendous boon electric lighting is
in these situations to the farm dweller.

The answer offered by Mr. Ripley, of Shenectady, N.Y., is practical and encouraging; it is a description of how he converted his ten-year-old six-room house into a model home by gradually adding electrical equipment without capital outlay, and, in his own words, proved that “ it costs less to live better.”

Three “ new ” livable rooms were gained because the new heating system was so clean and saved so much space; the house was much warmer; and the fuel bill went down nearly as much as the electricity bill went up. It is also thanks to the Dominions that we are now able to have dishes made from oysters and crawfish tails, when these are out of season in Great Britain, and many other delicacies not produced in this country.

article_title: EDITORIAL: Holiday Time at Home and Abroad
brief_extract: Boats, cars, electric trains which have the advantage of not covering their passengers with smuts, and aeroplanes, go speeding in all directions, while the persuasive publicity of travel agencies sets the imagination dancing with tantalising thoughts of mountains, forests and wide sea shores. For those who are going abroad in Europe, the opportunity to visit the Exhibition in Paris should not be missed, for it is an impressive conception and there is universal interest in the exhibits. Numerous congresses and subsidiary exhibitions are being held in connection with it, and as this magazine goes to press there is one in particular, the International Congress on Lighting Applications, which will have a special appeal for women.

location_standardised: Colombo, Western Province, Sri Lanka

brief_extract:
We had great fun trying to show off our
prowess with chop-sticks, learnt in Japan. We called at Colombo, in Ceylon, a lovely island of
queer shaped hills, coco-nut palms and blue sea, and
left the ship at Mombasa, where we spent two weeks
idling about the town, visiting native villages and, at
evening, swimming in the sea, protected from sharks by
the coral reef. Races are mixed in Mombasa; here, for
the first time, we saw the real African, tall, splay-footed,
woolly-haired and thick-lipped.

When we left Mombasa to travel south to the Cape
and up the west coast of Africa, the presence of a Moslem
celebrity on our ship called forth the Indian population
in large numbers, the women dressed in their beautiful
delicate-coloured robes of light green, pink and silver,

saw the cloves ripening on the trees among dark green

with the co-operation of the College Authorities. WHEN one visits the extensive and splendidly-
equipped buildings of the Glasgow and West
of Scotland College of Domestic Science to-day
and sees the 900 or so students training there for a wide
variety of careers, it is interesting to learn that this
modern organisation has over half a century's history
behind it and to know that the pride we take in our
Scottish educational institutions is amply justified in
the Domestic Science branch, for the Glasgow School of
Cookery was established as early as 1875, only two years
after the Kensington School in London. From the small philanthropic venture formed by some
prominent Glasgow citizens who were distressed at the
ignorance of cookery and nutrition prevailing among the
working women, the School has developed steadily for
62 years, always extending its premises, enlarging its
staff and increasing its scope.

FROM Frau Gisela Urban we have received an interesting description of the Institute for Life Economics that exists in Vienna to instruct future teachers or students at the University and the Academy of Arts in the natural sphere of women's work: life-economy. It is a culmination of the training that is given in all girls' schools, and in addition to domestic and nursing knowledge, is designed to instil an understanding of the vital necessities of life: how to provide for them in such a way that both those things that are indispensable and those that adorn human life are considered in the right proportion to each other; and to cater for all members of the family as a whole, at the same time respecting their individualities.

location_standardised: Hungary
brief_context: Subject of a talk by Miss Bogyo.
brief_extract: Ann's Passage, Manchester. The outstanding events of the Spring Programme were the Bristol Conference attended by 18 members from Manchester; the visit of Miss Bogyo, who gave an interesting talk and film on " Electricity in Hungary," followed by Hungarian dances in her national dress, to which we were pleased to welcome 150 members from neighbouring Branches in addition to 100 Manchester members; the successful Cold Party arranged by the Manchester Corporation, when we were told how to use the refrigerator and how to make cold sweets; and, most historically interesting, the visit to London on Coronation Day. The following account is extracted from a report written by one of the members who took part; unfortunately space prevents this from being given in full.

THE ELECTRICAL AGE. AUTUMN, 1937

EDITORIAL

THE third Summer School for Teachers arranged by the Electrical Association for Women was held this year in Glasgow from August 26th to 31st at the Glasgow and West of Scotland College of Domestic Science. Again there was a full complement of students wishing to learn something more of electrical housecraft, and it was noticeable, that with progress in the electrification of schools throughout the country, this course has passed beyond its early introductory stages and is advancing in educational usefulness to keep step with the needs and developing work of Domestic Subjects Teachers.

article_title: Novelties: In Arts and Techniques at the Paris Exhibition
brief_extract:
An all-glass house may seem a daring conception to
conservative minds. But to those who live in damp
northern climates and need all the available air, light
and warmth, the experiment presented by the French
firm of Saint Gobain in their striking pavilion 70 feet
high, built entirely of glass over an iron skeleton frame-
work, may suggest attractive possibilities when applied
to domestic architecture. Modern architects stress the utility of wide bays
inviting the free entry of nature's invigorating forces of
oxygen and ultra-violet rays.

location_standardised: Bohemia, Czech Republic
brief_context: Region noted for famous engraved crystal ware.
article_title: Novelties: In Arts and Techniques at the Paris Exhibition
brief_extract:
The Czecho-Slovakian Pavilion is also an all-glass
building on an iron frame, but of a more expensive type
suitable only for exhibition purposes. Here, alongside
the famous Bohemian engraved crystal ware, are to be
seen many novel uses of glass, such as the all-glass chair
and table, chess board and men, of beautiful effect in the
colour combination of luminous white, silver and rich
black, behind which stands a delightful screen of
engraved glass framed in nickel. Fireproof glass for
kitchen use has long ago convinced housewives of its
excellent properties, and many perfected examples can
be found in the Exhibition; also tea-services, cups and
saucers of delicate glass, enriched with silver designs,
look dainty on a glass-topped table, that fears neither
heat circles nor drops from flower bowls.

brief_extract:
AUTUMN, 1937

IN REVIEW

ONE of the Grand Old Men of the Electrical Industry, Sir Francis Fladgate, M.V.O., J.P., died this summer. He lived to be 84 and deserved the gratitude of London consumers for the work he did in promoting the organisation of electricity supply. He was an active leader of the Industry from 1890, first as a Director of Gatti Co., then as Chairman of its successor, The Charing Cross Company, and more latterly as a moving spirit in the formation of the London Electricity Joint Committee Ltd.
